title: Protocols of coherent motion control for an interaction-driven Rydberg gate
authors: Valentin Magro, Wojciech Adamczyk, Sylvain de Léséleuc
abstract: Generating entanglement between two Rydberg atoms is at the core of neutral-atom quantum computers. Current two-qubit gates operate in the Rydberg-blockade regime, in which the full strength of the van der Waals interaction between the two Rydberg atoms is not directly exploited, to avoid sensitivity to the position noise of the tweezer-trapped atoms, at the cost of a longer time spent in the Rydberg state. Here, we propose a set of techniques based on coherent control of the atomic motion obtained by combining optical tweezers and a two-dimensional optical lattice, and a sequence of multiple on/off pulses. The protocols keep the two-qubit gate error contribution from position noise below $10^{-4}$, heat the atom by less than~$Δn = 0.01$, while being robust to alignment errors of the potential up to $50$~nm and thermal excitation up to $\bar{n} = 3$. This toolbox opens the path for new two-qubit Rydberg gates directly, or partially, driven by the interaction, in which the atoms spend only $\sim 10$~ns in the Rydberg state, minimizing the increasingly dominant error source originating from its finite lifetime.
summary: The paper presents advanced protocols for realizing high-fidelity two-qubit gates in neutral atom quantum computers by exploiting direct interaction-driven coupling rather than relying solely on blockade physics. By integrating coherent control techniques like motion-echo sequences within optical lattices, the authors suppress detrimental errors arising from atomic position uncertainty and thermal motion to levels required for fault-tolerant computation.
main_problem: The primary goal is to achieve high-fidelity two-qubit entanglement gates for neutral atoms by moving beyond the limitations of the standard Rydberg-blockade regime.
main_result: The proposed protocols, combining coherent control of atomic motion with optical lattices and echo sequences, enable ultrafast interaction-driven gates with error contributions from position noise below $10^{-4}$.
method: The authors derive theoretical models for the motional propagator under an echo sequence and analyze gate infidelity by calculating expectation values for thermal and Fock states.
model_or_system: The system involves neutral atoms trapped in a combination of optical tweezers and superimposed two-dimensional optical lattices, utilizing Rydberg excitations to mediate entanglement.
key_observables: Gate fidelity ($F$), error contributions from position noise ($\Delta R$, $\delta R$), motional propagator expectation values, and residual displacement parameters ($\alpha_{	ext{res}}$).
important_parameters: Target error $1-F \lesssim 10^{-4}$, required static precision $\Delta R < 4$ nm, low heating rate ($\Delta n < 0.01$), and short Rydberg interaction time ($\sim 10$ ns).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to implement precise lattice loading and motion-echo sequences; error contributions are analyzed by treating various noise sources (static vs. thermal) independently.
figures_summary: Figure S2 provides an error budget comparing different gate protocols based on interatomic separation $R$, quantifying contributions from lifetime, static/thermal motion in x, y, and z directions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need to overcome Rydberg-blockade limitations (Chunk 1), then detailing how lattice confinement and echo sequences suppress position errors ($\Delta R$ and $\delta R$) down to required nanometer precision (Chunk 2). Finally, it provides rigorous theoretical derivations of the motional propagator and error budget analysis for these advanced protocols (Chunks 3 & 4).
why_interesting: This work represents a sophisticated blend of quantum control theory applied to atomic physics. The detailed mathematical treatment of motion-echo sequences and the quantitative error budgeting against multiple noise sources (thermal, static) is highly relevant for designing next-generation quantum hardware.
